quote: Example 4.1. Let Xi, i = 1, 2, have Pareto type II survival function F̄Xi(t) = (1 + t/βi)^{−αi}, αi > 1, βi > 0, t ≥ 0. If β1 ≥ β2, then X1 ≤MRLAI X2.
compared: two Pareto II variables ordered by scale parameter β

quote: Theorem 4.1. For two lifetime random variables X and Y, X ≤MRLAI Y if and only if AX(t)/AY(t) is nonincreasing on (0, τXY).
compared: X vs Y in the MRLAI order (X ≤MRLAI Y iff LµX ≤ LµY pointwise)

hypotheses.text: lifetime random variables, τXY = min{τX, τY}

conclusion.direction: X <=MRLAI Y iff AX(t)/AY(t) nonincreasing on (0, τXY)

quote: Theorem 4.2. Let X and Y have positive continuous MRL functions on (0, τX) and (0, τY), respectively. If µX(t)/µY(t) is nonincreasing on (0, τXY), then X ≤MRLAI Y.
compared: MRL-ratio monotonicity as sufficient condition for MRLAI order

quote: Theorem 4.3. Let X and Y have positive continuous MRL functions on (0, τX) and (0, τY), respectively. Then, for each fixed 0 < a < τXY, Xa ≤MRLAI Ya if and only if [AX(a + s) − AX(a)]/[AY(a + s) − AY(a)] is nonincreasing on (0, τXY − a).
model: residual lifetimes Xa = (X − a|X > a), Ya

conclusion.direction: Xa <=MRLAI Ya iff the increment-ratio is nonincreasing

quote: Corollary 4.3.1. Let X and Y have positive continuous MRL functions on (0, τX) and (0, τY), respectively. If µX(t)/µY(t) is nonincreasing on (0, τXY), then Xa ≤MRLAI Ya for every 0 < a < τXY.
compared: sufficient condition for MRLAI order of all residual lifetimes

conclusion.direction: Xa <=MRLAI Ya for every a in (0, τXY)

ambiguity: Condition is only sufficient (Counterexample 4.1 shows failure of preservation in general).

quote: Counterexample 4.1. Let Y be an exponential random variable with mean one. ... Let X have the MRL function µX(t) = 1 − 0.4t (0 ≤ t < 2), 0.1t (2 ≤ t < 3), 0.3 (t ≥ 3). ... Hence LµX(t) < 1 = LµY(t) for all t > 0, and therefore X ≤MRLAI Y. ... Consequently, X2 ≰MRLAI Y2, although X ≤MRLAI Y. Therefore, the MRLAI order is not preserved under residual-lifetime transformation in general.
model: X with piecewise-linear MRL vs exponential Y; residual lifetimes at age a = 2
compared: X ≤MRLAI Y but residual lifetime comparison fails

conclusion.direction: X <=MRLAI Y but X2 not <=MRLAI Y2 (LµX2(s) = (4+2s)/(4+s) > 1 for 0 < s < 1)

quote: Counterexample 4.2. Let X be an exponential random variable having failure rate 0.5, and let Y be another random variable having survival function F̄Y(t) = (t + 1)^{−3}, for t ≥ 0. Then, we have LµX(t) = 1 and LµY(t) = 2(t + 1)/(t + 2), for t ≥ 0, so that X ≤MRLAI Y. However, X ≰icx Y since ∫_t^∞ F̄X − ∫_t^∞ F̄Y = 2e^{−t/2} − 1/{2(t+1)²} equals 0.6802033 at t = 2 and −0.001138222 at t = 18. Moreover, µX(1) = 2 > µY(1) = 1, and hence X ≰mrl Y.
compared: MRLAI order holds but icx and mrl fail

conclusion.direction: X <=MRLAI Y but X not <=icx Y and X not <=mrl Y

numbers: icx integral difference: 0.6802033 at t=2, −0.001138222 at t=18; µX(1) = 2 > µY(1) = 1

quote: Counterexample 4.3. Let X have survival function F̄X(t) = (t² + 2t + 2)e^{−t}/2, and let Y have Pareto survival function F̄Y(t) = (t + 1)^{−3}, t ≥ 0. ... It can be verified that LµX(t) ≤ LµY(t) for all t > 0, so that X ≤MRLAI Y. ... Then b(0.40) = 13.66380, b(0.80) = 14.10533, and b(1.5) = 12.96944. Since the ratio required for the vrl order is 1/b(t), and 1/b(0.40) > 1/b(0.80), we have X ≰vrl Y.
family: X: F̄ = (t²+2t+2)e^{−t}/2 (Gamma-2 mixture form); Y: Pareto (t+1)^{−3}

conclusion.direction: X <=MRLAI Y but X not <=vrl Y

quote: Counterexample 4.4. Let X and Y have Erlang densities fX(t) = 9te^{−3t} and fY(t) = 4te^{−2t}, t ≥ 0, respectively. ... Hence X ≤vrl Y. On the other hand ... R(t) = 4{3t + ln(3t + 1)}/{9{2t + ln(2t + 1)}}. Since R(0.1) = 0.653742 > R(1.5) = 0.628701 < R(5) = 0.637118, R(t) is not nonincreasing. Therefore X ≰MRLAI Y, showing that X ≤vrl Y ⇏ X ≤MRLAI Y.
compared: vrl order holds but MRLAI fails

conclusion.direction: X <=vrl Y but X not <=MRLAI Y

quote: Counterexample 4.5. Let X and Y be two independent random variables having Erlang distribution with respective density functions fX(t) = 9te^{−3t}, t ≥ 0 and fY(t) = 4te^{−2t}, t ≥ 0. It is easy to see that X ⩽lr Y. However, [integrated-MRL ratio] = 4{3t + ln(3t + 1)}/{9{2t + ln(2t + 1)}} = 0.65370 (t = 0.1), 0.6287006 (t = 1.5), 0.6371185 (t = 5). Thus, we have X ≤lr Y ⇏ X ≤MRLAI Y.

conclusion.direction: X <=lr Y but X not <=MRLAI Y; hence none of hr, st, mrl, vrl, icx implies MRLAI

quote: Theorem 4.4. Let X and Y be lifetime random variables. If X is DMRLA and Y is IMRLA, then X ≤MRLAI Y.
family: DMRLA class vs IMRLA class (decreasing/increasing MRL ageing intensity)

quote: Counterexample 4.6. Let X and Y have MRL functions µX(t) = 1 + t and µY(t) = 1 + 3t, respectively, for t ≥ 0. Then LµX(t) = 2(t + 1)/(t + 2) and LµY(t) = 2(1 + 3t)/(2 + 3t), t > 0. Since LµY(t) − LµX(t) = 4t/{(t + 2)(3t + 2)} > 0 for all t > 0, we have X ≤MRLAI Y. However, both X and Y are IMRLA, showing that the sufficient condition in the preceding theorem is not necessary.

conclusion.direction: X <=MRLAI Y holds without Theorem 4.4's class dichotomy (non-necessity)

quote: Corollary 4.4.1. If X is decreasing in MRL and Y is increasing in MRL then X ≤MRLAI Y.
compared: MRL monotonicity classes imply MRLAI order

quote: Theorem 4.5. Let {Xi, i = 1, . . . , m} and {Yj, j = 1, . . . , n} be two sets of independent and identically distributed random variables with MRL functions µXi(t) = a + bt and µYj(t) = c + dt, respectively, where a, c > 0 and b, d ≥ 0. Then (i) Xi ≤MRLAI Yj if and only if ad − bc ≥ 0. (ii) If Xi ≤MRLAI Yj, then for all m, n ≥ 1, X(m) = min Xi ≤MRLAI Y(n) = min Yj.
family: linear-MRL family µ(t) = a + bt (Pareto-type survival F̄ = (1 + bt/a)^{−(1+1/b)})
compared: component-level MRLAI order iff ad − bc ≥ 0, and preservation under series formation

hypotheses.text: µXi = a + bt, µYj = c + dt; a, c > 0, b, d ≥ 0

conclusion.direction: (i) Xi <=MRLAI Yj iff ad − bc >= 0; (ii) then X(m) <=MRLAI Y(n) for all m, n (Lµ invariant under series formation)

quote: Counterexample 4.7. Let X1 and X2 be two i.i.d. random variables having Erlang distribution with survival function F̄Xi(t) = (1 + t)e^{−t}, t ≥ 0. Also, let Y1 and Y2 be two i.i.d. random variables having exponential distribution with survival function F̄Yi(t) = e^{−2t}, t ≥ 0. ... Thus Xi ≤MRLAI Yj for all i, j = 1, 2. If we write X = max{X1, X2} and Y = max{Y1, Y2} ... the curves of LµX(t) and LµY(t) intersect. Therefore, the MRLAI order is not preserved under the formation of a parallel system.
family: Xi iid Erlang-2(rate 1); Yi iid Exp(rate 2)
compared: componentwise MRLAI order fails to propagate to maxima

conclusion.direction: Xi <=MRLAI Yj for all i,j but LµX and LµY of the maxima cross — X not <=MRLAI Y

quote: Theorem 4.6. Let X and Y be non-negative continuous random variables such that X ≤MRLAI Y. Then, for every a > 0, the MRLAI order is preserved under the transformation ϕ(x) = ax, that is, ϕ(X) ≤MRLAI ϕ(Y).
compared: closure of MRLAI order under common positive scaling

quote: Counterexample 4.8. Let X and Y be two non-negative random variables with F̄X(0) = F̄Y(0) = 1 and MRL functions µX(t) = 10 + t, and µY(t) = 1 + 0.2t, for t ≥ 0 ... It can be verified algebraically that LµX(t) < LµY(t) for all t > 0, showing that X ≤MRLAI Y. Now, consider the affine transformation ϕ(x) = x + 2 ... The two functions cross at t = (8 + 2√226)/5 ... Therefore, the order is not preserved under the affine shift ϕ(x) = x + 2.
model: two lifetime distributions under affine shift
compared: X ≤MRLAI Y but shifted versions not ordered

conclusion.direction: X <=MRLAI Y but U not <=MRLAI V — order not preserved under affine shifts
